text.ch-anatomy:
CHAPTER 1 OF 5 · AIRWAY BLOCKS FOR AWAKE INTUBATION

Anatomy: sensory supply of the airway

Three cranial nerves supply the airway: the trigeminal (V), the glossopharyngeal (IX) and the vagus (X).

Airway, midline section

Nasal cavity (V1 anterior ethmoidal, V2 palatine): nasal mucosa and septum
Oropharynx (IX glossopharyngeal, X pharyngeal): back of the tongue, vallecula, tonsils, pharyngeal walls; the gag reflex
Vocal cords and below (X recurrent laryngeal): cords, subglottis and trachea
Anterior two-thirds of the tongue (V3 lingual): front of the tongue
Larynx above the cords (X internal superior laryngeal): back of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids

Fill patterns here separate neighbouring regions only (solid: nose, oropharynx, cords and trachea; hatched: tongue and larynx above the cords). Midline section, schematic.

REGION	NERVE	HOW TO ANAESTHETISE IT
Nose
Anterior ethmoidal (V1); greater and lesser palatine (V2), via the pterygopalatine (sphenopalatine) ganglion behind the middle turbinate
Co-phenylcaine spray; soaked pledgets or cotton applicators
Front two-thirds of the tongue
Lingual (V3)
Spray, gargle, paste
Back of the tongue, vallecula, front of the epiglottis, tonsils
Glossopharyngeal (IX)
Spray the tonsillar pillars; glossopharyngeal block
Pharyngeal walls
Vagus (X), pharyngeal branch
Spray the walls
Larynx above the cords
Internal superior laryngeal (X)
Spray-as-you-go; superior laryngeal block

text.ch-topical:
CHAPTER 2 OF 5 · AIRWAY BLOCKS FOR AWAKE INTUBATION

Topical anaesthesia for awake intubation

Topical anaesthesia is the mainstay of awake tracheal intubation; nerve blocks are added when it is not enough.

BEFORE YOU START

Maximum topical lidocaine: 9 mg/kg in adults (4.5 mg/kg in children). About 25% is absorbed from the upper airway, which is why this is higher than the dose for infiltration.
Clear blood, secretions and vomit first: the drug has to touch the mucosa.
Trismus: sprays and blocks inside the mouth may be impossible. Use nebulised lidocaine or a transtracheal injection.
Check the topical anaesthesia works before you start (for example, a gentle suction catheter or oral airway is tolerated).
Drugs
PREPARATION	STRENGTH	NOTES
Lidocaine solution
1%, 2% or 4%
Spray-as-you-go, nebuliser, atomiser, transtracheal
Lidocaine spray
10% (10 mg per spray)
Count the sprays
Co-phenylcaine
Lidocaine 5% with phenylephrine 0.5%: 5 mg lidocaine and 0.5 mg phenylephrine per spray
Nose: anaesthesia and vasoconstriction together
Lidocaine gel or paste
Applicators and pledgets
Cocaine
5% or 10%; maximum 1.5 mg/kg
The only local anaesthetic that is also a vasoconstrictor; more cardiovascular side effects
Vasoconstrictor
Xylometazoline or phenylephrine
Essential in the nose: less bleeding and more room. Allow time to work.
Ways to apply it
METHOD	HOW	GOOD FOR
Nebuliser
5 ml of 4% lidocaine with oxygen over up to 30 minutes; patient sitting up
Whole airway, non-invasive; trismus
Spray from the container
Long nozzle into the nose and mouth
Nose and oropharynx
Atomiser (MAD)
Mist from a device on the end of a syringe
Nose and mouth
McKenzie technique
20G cannula joined by a three-way tap to oxygen tubing at 2–4 l/min; inject lidocaine slowly through the top port for a jet spray
Directed spray to the nose and mouth
Spray-as-you-go
2% or 4% lidocaine through the working channel of the scope, or an epidural catheter fed down it
Larynx, cords and trachea, under vision
Direct contact
Ribbon gauze or cotton applicators soaked in local anaesthetic or paste
Targeted: nose, tonsillar pillars, piriform fossae

WARNING

Topical anaesthesia removes protective reflexes

Cough and swallow are blunted, so the patient can aspirate. Topical anaesthesia of the pharynx can also cause brief airway obstruction, from loss of the reflexes that keep the glottis open.

CHAPTER 3 OF 5 · AIRWAY · ABOVE THE CORDS

Superior laryngeal nerve block

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (X) supplies the larynx above the vocal cords: the base of the tongue, the back of the epiglottis, the aryepiglottic folds and the arytenoids. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane 2–4 mm below the greater cornu of the hyoid.

USE IT FOR

Awake tracheal intubation (both sides), when topical anaesthesia alone is not enough
Awake laryngoscopy and laryngeal procedures
POSITION
Supine, neck slightly extended
PROBE
Linear, parasagittal between the hyoid and thyroid cartilage (or landmarks)
NEEDLE
25G
DOSE
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side
COVERS
The larynx above the vocal cords

Position

Supine with the neck slightly extended, so you can feel the hyoid.

Equipment
25G needle; linear probe if using ultrasound
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (1–2 ml with ultrasound).
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (external) approach. Feel the hyoid and push it gently towards the side you are blocking. Insert the needle from the side, aiming at the greater cornu. Once you touch it, walk the needle off its lower edge and inject 2 ml: this blocks both the internal and external branches. Advance a few millimetres more and you feel a “give” through the thyrohyoid membrane; injecting there blocks only the internal branch.

If the hyoid is hard to feel, use the superior cornu of the thyroid cartilage instead (follow the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage back from the notch), walk off it upwards, and inject 2 ml through the membrane and 2 ml as you withdraw.

Ultrasound. Useful when the landmarks are hard to feel. Find the greater cornu of the hyoid and the thyrohyoid membrane; the nerve runs with the superior laryngeal artery just below the greater cornu. Inject 1–2 ml there.

Without a needle (internal approach): gauze soaked in local anaesthetic held in each piriform fossa with Krause’s forceps for 5–10 minutes.

Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane from caudal, or out-of-plane. Aim just below the greater cornu, superficial to the thyrohyoid membrane, beside the artery.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Strap muscles
Thyrohyoid muscle
Pre-epiglottic fat
Target and deposition

The space between the thyrohyoid muscle and the thyrohyoid membrane, just below the greater cornu. The success rate with ultrasound is over 90%; failures are put down to variation in the nerve’s position.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side

Both sides.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Larynx above the cords (X internal superior laryngeal): back of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids

Covers: The larynx above the vocal cords (both sides blocked).

MECHANISM

The internal branch carries sensation from the larynx above the cords; it is blocked where it goes through the thyrohyoid membrane.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense when both sides are blocked. Combine with topical anaesthesia of the mouth and pharynx and a transtracheal block (or spray-as-you-go) for the cords and trachea.

WHAT IT MISSES
The vocal cords and trachea (recurrent laryngeal nerve): add a transtracheal block.
The oropharynx and the gag reflex (glossopharyngeal nerve).
The nose.
Complications and how to avoid them
Intravascular injection: the superior laryngeal artery is next to the nerve and the carotid is nearby. Aspirate.
Aspiration risk: the larynx above the cords can no longer protect the airway. Use with care in a patient with a full stomach.
Practical pearls
Push the hyoid towards the side you are blocking: the greater cornu becomes easier to feel.
The external branch is motor to cricothyroid; blocking it can change the voice. That is expected.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Describe the sensory supply of the airway. Which nerves would you block for an awake fibreoptic intubation, and how?

Model answer points
Nose: anterior ethmoidal (V1) and palatine nerves (V2). Topical (co-phenylcaine, soaked pledgets).
Mouth and pharynx: lingual (V3) front of tongue; glossopharyngeal (IX) back of tongue, vallecula, front of epiglottis, tonsils, gag reflex; vagus (X) pharyngeal walls.
Larynx above the cords: internal superior laryngeal nerve (X). Block at the greater cornu of the hyoid, 2 ml 2% lidocaine each side.
Cords and trachea: recurrent laryngeal nerve (X). Never block it directly (bilateral cord palsy). Use a transtracheal injection of 4% lidocaine or spray-as-you-go.
Total lidocaine within 9 mg/kg.

CHAPTER 4 OF 5 · AIRWAY · BELOW THE CORDS

Transtracheal (translaryngeal) block

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the vocal cords and trachea. It is never blocked directly: its motor and sensory fibres run together, so a block on both sides would paralyse both cords. Instead, local anaesthetic is injected into the trachea through the cricothyroid membrane.

USE IT FOR

Awake tracheal intubation
Trismus or limited mouth opening, where sprays can’t reach the larynx
POSITION
Supine, neck extended
PROBE
Linear, longitudinal in the midline (or landmarks)
NEEDLE
20–22G, on a syringe
DOSE
5 ml of 4% lidocaine
COVERS
Vocal cords and trachea (and some spread above the cords with coughing)

Transtracheal block: sagittal midline view of the cricothyroid membrane

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine with the neck extended. Feel the thyroid cartilage in the midline and move down to the cricoid; the membrane is the dip between them, just above the cricoid. Stabilise the larynx with thumb and middle finger.

Equipment
20 or 22G needle on a 5 or 10 ml syringe
5 ml of 4% lidocaine.
Landmarks and scanning

Feel, or find with ultrasound, the cricothyroid membrane. With the probe longitudinal in the midline, count up from the tracheal rings to the cricoid, then the membrane, then the thyroid cartilage; mark the membrane on the skin.

Needle approach

Perpendicular to the skin in the midline, aspirating continuously. Air bubbles mean you are in the trachea: stop advancing, so the needle does not hit the back wall of the trachea.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Target and deposition

The lumen of the trachea, just below the cords. Inject quickly; the cough that follows spreads the local anaesthetic.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

5 ml of 4% lidocaine (200 mg)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Variable: patchy, not reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Vocal cords and below (X recurrent laryngeal): cords, subglottis and trachea
Larynx above the cords (X internal superior laryngeal): back of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids

Covers: The vocal cords and the trachea; some spread above the cords with coughing.

MECHANISM

Topical anaesthesia from inside the airway, spread by the cough.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense for the cords and trachea. Above the cords it is patchy: add a superior laryngeal block or spray-as-you-go.

WHAT IT MISSES
The nose, mouth and pharynx.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bleeding into the airway; puncture of the back wall of the trachea or oesophagus if the needle is advanced after air is aspirated.
Coughing: undesirable with an unstable neck, raised intracranial or intraocular pressure.
Loss of airway reflexes: a risk with a full stomach.
Practical pearls
Finding the cricothyroid membrane with ultrasound is the same skill you need for an emergency front-of-neck airway. Practise it.
Warn the patient that they will cough.

text.ch-gpn:
CHAPTER 5 OF 5 · AIRWAY · OROPHARYNX

Glossopharyngeal nerve block

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) supplies the back third of the tongue, the vallecula, the front of the epiglottis and the tonsils, and is the sensory limb of the gag reflex. It is easiest to block where it runs along the base of the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (the tonsillar pillars). This abolishes the gag, but on its own is not enough for an awake intubation.

USE IT FOR

Awake fibreoptic intubation through the mouth, when the gag reflex is a problem
Awake laryngoscopy, tonsillar procedures
POSITION
Sitting or supine, mouth open
PROBE
None: intraoral landmarks
NEEDLE
22–25G (or soaked gauze)
DOSE
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (intraoral)
COVERS
Back of the tongue, vallecula, tonsils; the gag reflex
Position

Mouth open wide enough to see the base of the tonsillar pillars. Spray the mouth with lidocaine first.

Equipment
Tongue depressor or a laryngoscope blade
22–25G needle, or ribbon gauze soaked in local anaesthetic
Technique

Intraoral. After topical spray, push the tongue to the other side with a tongue depressor. Insert the needle submucosally at the base of the posterior tonsillar pillar (or the anterior pillar), about 0.5 cm lateral to the side of the tongue where it meets the floor of the mouth. Aspirate, then inject 2 ml of 2% lidocaine. Repeat on the other side.

Without a needle: hold gauze soaked in local anaesthetic firmly on the same spot for a few minutes. Safer (no risk of carotid injection) but less effective.

Peristyloid approach (rarely used): the styloid process lies halfway along a line from the angle of the jaw to the mastoid tip. Touch it (1–2 cm deep), walk off it posteriorly, and inject after aspirating. The internal carotid artery is right there.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (intraoral)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Oropharynx (IX glossopharyngeal, X pharyngeal): back of the tongue, vallecula, tonsils, pharyngeal walls; the gag reflex

Covers: Back of the tongue, vallecula, front of the epiglottis, tonsils; the gag reflex.

MECHANISM

The nerve is just under the mucosa at the base of the tonsillar pillars.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Abolishes the gag reflex. Does not cover the larynx.

WHAT IT MISSES
The larynx above and below the cords.
The front of the tongue (lingual nerve) and the nose.
Complications and how to avoid them
Carotid artery injection: the internal carotid is close behind the tonsillar pillar. Aspirate before injecting.
Loss of the gag and swallowing reflexes: aspiration risk.

Probe parasagittal on the side of the neck, between the hyoid and the thyroid cartilage. Find the bright greater cornu of the hyoid (cranially, with a shadow) and the thyroid cartilage (caudally).

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Between them: the thin thyrohyoid muscle over the bright thyrohyoid membrane, and pre-epiglottic fat deep to it. Aspirate (the artery is right there), then inject 1–2 ml. The fluid lifts the muscle off the membrane. Repeat on the other side.

Cough and swallow are blunted, so the patient can aspirate. Topical anaesthesia of the pharynx can also cause brief airway obstruction, from loss of the reflexes that keep the glottis open.

CHAPTER 3 OF 5 · AIRWAY · ABOVE THE CORDS

Superior laryngeal nerve block

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (X) supplies the larynx above the vocal cords: the base of the tongue, the back of the epiglottis, the aryepiglottic folds and the arytenoids. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane 2–4 mm below the greater cornu of the hyoid.

USE IT FOR

Awake tracheal intubation (both sides), when topical anaesthesia alone is not enough
Awake laryngoscopy and laryngeal procedures
POSITION
Supine, neck slightly extended
PROBE
Linear, parasagittal between the hyoid and thyroid cartilage (or landmarks)
NEEDLE
25G
DOSE
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side
COVERS
The larynx above the vocal cords

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine with the neck slightly extended, so you can feel the hyoid.

Equipment
25G needle; linear probe if using ultrasound
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (1–2 ml with ultrasound).
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (external) approach. Feel the hyoid and push it gently towards the side you are blocking. Insert the needle from the side, aiming at the greater cornu. Once you touch it, walk the needle off its lower edge and inject 2 ml: this blocks both the internal and external branches. Advance a few millimetres more and you feel a “give” through the thyrohyoid membrane; injecting there blocks only the internal branch.

If the hyoid is hard to feel, use the superior cornu of the thyroid cartilage instead (follow the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage back from the notch), walk off it upwards, and inject 2 ml through the membrane and 2 ml as you withdraw.

Ultrasound. Useful when the landmarks are hard to feel. Find the greater cornu of the hyoid and the thyrohyoid membrane; the nerve runs with the superior laryngeal artery just below the greater cornu. Inject 1–2 ml there.

Without a needle (internal approach): gauze soaked in local anaesthetic held in each piriform fossa with Krause’s forceps for 5–10 minutes.

Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane from caudal, or out-of-plane. Aim just below the greater cornu, superficial to the thyrohyoid membrane, beside the artery.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Strap muscles
Thyrohyoid muscle
Pre-epiglottic fat
Target and deposition

The space between the thyrohyoid muscle and the thyrohyoid membrane, just below the greater cornu. The success rate with ultrasound is over 90%; failures are put down to variation in the nerve’s position.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side

Both sides.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Larynx above the cords (X internal superior laryngeal): back of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids

Covers: The larynx above the vocal cords (both sides blocked).

MECHANISM

The internal branch carries sensation from the larynx above the cords; it is blocked where it goes through the thyrohyoid membrane.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense when both sides are blocked. Combine with topical anaesthesia of the mouth and pharynx and a transtracheal block (or spray-as-you-go) for the cords and trachea.

WHAT IT MISSES
The vocal cords and trachea (recurrent laryngeal nerve): add a transtracheal block.
The oropharynx and the gag reflex (glossopharyngeal nerve).
The nose.
Complications and how to avoid them
Intravascular injection: the superior laryngeal artery is next to the nerve and the carotid is nearby. Aspirate.
Aspiration risk: the larynx above the cords can no longer protect the airway. Use with care in a patient with a full stomach.
Practical pearls
Push the hyoid towards the side you are blocking: the greater cornu becomes easier to feel.
The external branch is motor to cricothyroid; blocking it can change the voice. That is expected.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Describe the sensory supply of the airway. Which nerves would you block for an awake fibreoptic intubation, and how?

Model answer points
Nose: anterior ethmoidal (V1) and palatine nerves (V2). Topical (co-phenylcaine, soaked pledgets).
Mouth and pharynx: lingual (V3) front of tongue; glossopharyngeal (IX) back of tongue, vallecula, front of epiglottis, tonsils, gag reflex; vagus (X) pharyngeal walls.
Larynx above the cords: internal superior laryngeal nerve (X). Block at the greater cornu of the hyoid, 2 ml 2% lidocaine each side.
Cords and trachea: recurrent laryngeal nerve (X). Never block it directly (bilateral cord palsy). Use a transtracheal injection of 4% lidocaine or spray-as-you-go.
Total lidocaine within 9 mg/kg.

CHAPTER 4 OF 5 · AIRWAY · BELOW THE CORDS

Transtracheal (translaryngeal) block

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the vocal cords and trachea. It is never blocked directly: its motor and sensory fibres run together, so a block on both sides would paralyse both cords. Instead, local anaesthetic is injected into the trachea through the cricothyroid membrane.

USE IT FOR

Awake tracheal intubation
Trismus or limited mouth opening, where sprays can’t reach the larynx
POSITION
Supine, neck extended
PROBE
Linear, longitudinal in the midline (or landmarks)
NEEDLE
20–22G, on a syringe
DOSE
5 ml of 4% lidocaine
COVERS
Vocal cords and trachea (and some spread above the cords with coughing)

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine with the neck extended. Feel the thyroid cartilage in the midline and move down to the cricoid; the membrane is the dip between them, just above the cricoid. Stabilise the larynx with thumb and middle finger.

Equipment
20 or 22G needle on a 5 or 10 ml syringe
5 ml of 4% lidocaine.
Landmarks and scanning

Feel, or find with ultrasound, the cricothyroid membrane. With the probe longitudinal in the midline, count up from the tracheal rings to the cricoid, then the membrane, then the thyroid cartilage; mark the membrane on the skin.

Needle approach

Perpendicular to the skin in the midline, aspirating continuously. Air bubbles mean you are in the trachea: stop advancing, so the needle does not hit the back wall of the trachea.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Target and deposition

The lumen of the trachea, just below the cords. Inject quickly; the cough that follows spreads the local anaesthetic.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

5 ml of 4% lidocaine (200 mg)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Variable: patchy, not reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Vocal cords and below (X recurrent laryngeal): cords, subglottis and trachea
Larynx above the cords (X internal superior laryngeal): back of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids

Covers: The vocal cords and the trachea; some spread above the cords with coughing.

MECHANISM

Topical anaesthesia from inside the airway, spread by the cough.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense for the cords and trachea. Above the cords it is patchy: add a superior laryngeal block or spray-as-you-go.

WHAT IT MISSES
The nose, mouth and pharynx.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bleeding into the airway; puncture of the back wall of the trachea or oesophagus if the needle is advanced after air is aspirated.
Coughing: undesirable with an unstable neck, raised intracranial or intraocular pressure.
Loss of airway reflexes: a risk with a full stomach.
Practical pearls
Finding the cricothyroid membrane with ultrasound is the same skill you need for an emergency front-of-neck airway. Practise it.
Warn the patient that they will cough.

text.ch-gpn:
CHAPTER 5 OF 5 · AIRWAY · OROPHARYNX

Glossopharyngeal nerve block

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) supplies the back third of the tongue, the vallecula, the front of the epiglottis and the tonsils, and is the sensory limb of the gag reflex. It is easiest to block where it runs along the base of the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (the tonsillar pillars). This abolishes the gag, but on its own is not enough for an awake intubation.

USE IT FOR

Awake fibreoptic intubation through the mouth, when the gag reflex is a problem
Awake laryngoscopy, tonsillar procedures
POSITION
Sitting or supine, mouth open
PROBE
None: intraoral landmarks
NEEDLE
22–25G (or soaked gauze)
DOSE
2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (intraoral)
COVERS
Back of the tongue, vallecula, tonsils; the gag reflex
Position

Mouth open wide enough to see the base of the tonsillar pillars. Spray the mouth with lidocaine first.

Equipment
Tongue depressor or a laryngoscope blade
22–25G needle, or ribbon gauze soaked in local anaesthetic
Technique

Intraoral. After topical spray, push the tongue to the other side with a tongue depressor. Insert the needle submucosally at the base of the posterior tonsillar pillar (or the anterior pillar), about 0.5 cm lateral to the side of the tongue where it meets the floor of the mouth. Aspirate, then inject 2 ml of 2% lidocaine. Repeat on the other side.

Without a needle: hold gauze soaked in local anaesthetic firmly on the same spot for a few minutes. Safer (no risk of carotid injection) but less effective.

Peristyloid approach (rarely used): the styloid process lies halfway along a line from the angle of the jaw to the mastoid tip. Touch it (1–2 cm deep), walk off it posteriorly, and inject after aspirating. The internal carotid artery is right there.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

2 ml of 2% lidocaine per side (intraoral)

Local anaesthetic toxicity: All the lidocaine counts: sprays, nebuliser, blocks and transtracheal injection together. Keep the total within 9 mg/kg (adults; 4.5 mg/kg in children).

Coverage

Airway, midline section

Dense: reliable
Midline structures. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Oropharynx (IX glossopharyngeal, X pharyngeal): back of the tongue, vallecula, tonsils, pharyngeal walls; the gag reflex

Covers: Back of the tongue, vallecula, front of the epiglottis, tonsils; the gag reflex.

MECHANISM

The nerve is just under the mucosa at the base of the tonsillar pillars.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Abolishes the gag reflex. Does not cover the larynx.

WHAT IT MISSES
The larynx above and below the cords.
The front of the tongue (lingual nerve) and the nose.
Complications and how to avoid them
Carotid artery injection: the internal carotid is close behind the tonsillar pillar. Aspirate before injecting.
Loss of the gag and swallowing reflexes: aspiration risk.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe parasagittal on the side of the neck, between the hyoid and the thyroid cartilage. Find the bright greater cornu of the hyoid (cranially, with a shadow) and the thyroid cartilage (caudally).

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Between them: the thin thyrohyoid muscle over the bright thyrohyoid membrane, and pre-epiglottic fat deep to it. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior laryngeal artery just below the greater cornu, between the muscle and the membrane. Find the artery with colour Doppler.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane from caudal (or out-of-plane), to the space between the thyrohyoid muscle and the membrane, next to the artery, just below the greater cornu. If you pass through the membrane, you are in the pre-epiglottic space: withdraw.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate (the artery is right there), then inject 1–2 ml. The fluid lifts the muscle off the membrane. Repeat on the other side.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe longitudinal in the midline. Start low and count the tracheal rings (dark beads), then slide up: the cricoid is bigger and more superficial, and above it the cricothyroid membrane, then the thyroid cartilage. Mark the membrane on the skin.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

The cartilages are dark (hypoechoic) with a thin bright edge. Deep to them, the bright air–mucosa line with repeated reverberation lines below: everything under it is artefact from air. The membrane is the bright band between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

Stabilise the larynx with thumb and middle finger. A 20–22G needle on a syringe of local anaesthetic, perpendicular in the midline just above the cricoid, aspirating as you go. Air bubbles mean the tip is in the trachea: stop advancing at once, so you do not puncture the back wall.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Inject 5 ml of 4% lidocaine quickly, then take the needle out. The patient coughs, which spreads the local anaesthetic up to the cords and down the trachea. Press on the site.
